title: Daily price jump
topic: A loop over `range(len(prices) - 1)` that looks one short
blurb: A helper scanning consecutive days for the largest price increase.
prompt: Spec: return the largest single-day increase (`prices[i+1] - prices[i]`), or `0` if prices never rose or fewer than 2 days exist. Review this helper — tap a line if it breaks the spec, or let it pass.
conclusion: AI summary: Checks every consecutive day pair and returns the largest positive jump, or 0 for short/falling series.

diagnosis: Accepting `prices` without a default `prices=[]` causes a TypeError if called with an empty list.
Function signature should annotate `prices: list[float]` or Python treats entries as strings.
Passing a list by reference here lets the loop overwrite `prices` in place.
`max_daily_jump` shadows Python's built-in `max` function.
fix: Change the signature to `def max_daily_jump(prices=None):`.
Clone `prices = list(prices)` before iterating.
Add type annotations `prices: list[float] -> float`.
Rename the helper so it doesn't start with `max_`.

diagnosis: Checking `len(prices) < 2` rejects two-day inputs when `len(prices) == 2`.
Should be `len(prices) <= 2` because two prices only form one jump, not a max.
If `prices` is empty `[]`, `len(prices)` raises an IndexError before `< 2` runs.
Checking `< 2` skips the case where prices drop on every day.
fix: Change the guard to `if len(prices) <= 1:` and handle `len == 2` separately.
Change `< 2` to `<= 2` so two-day lists return early.
Check `if prices is None or len(prices) == 0:` instead of `< 2`.
Remove the guard — the loop already handles single-element lists.

diagnosis: Returning `0` for fewer than 2 days hides missing data; it should return `None`.
Returning integer `0` breaks float callers when `prices` holds decimals.
Returning `0` here exits before checking if `prices[0]` is positive.
Returning early inside `if` prevents `best` from ever being initialized.
fix: Return `None` instead of `0` when fewer than 2 days are passed.
Return `0.0` so the return type is always float.
Return `prices[0]` for a single-day list.
Initialize `best = 0` before the `if` check.

diagnosis: Initializing `best = 0` breaks when every daily change is negative — it should start at `float('-inf')`.
Setting `best = 0` ignores the first day's price `prices[0]` as a starting baseline.
`best` should start at `prices[1] - prices[0]` or the first pair never gets compared.
Starting `best` at `0` means a 0-dollar jump can't be distinguished from an empty list.
fix: Initialize `best = float('-inf')` so negative daily drops are preserved.
Initialize `best = prices[0]` before starting the loop.
Set `best = prices[1] - prices[0]` and start the loop at index `1`.
Initialize `best = None` and update on the first iteration.

diagnosis: Off-by-one: `range(len(prices) - 1)` stops before the last element, silently dropping the final day's jump.
`range(len(prices) - 1)` runs 0 times on a 2-element list, returning 0 for `[10, 25]`.
Subtracting 1 from `len(prices)` makes `i` negative when `prices` has length 1.
Using `range(len(prices) - 1)` skips `prices[0]` because Python stops short on both ends.
fix: Use `for i in range(len(prices)):` so the last day is included.
Use `for i in range(1, len(prices)):` to cover the last element.
Use `for i in range(len(prices) + 1):` so the final index isn't dropped.
Iterate with `for price in prices:` instead of indexing.

diagnosis: Subtracting `prices[i + 1] - prices[i]` reads past the end of the list on the final iteration.
The subtraction is reversed — it should be `prices[i] - prices[i + 1]` for a price jump.
Computing `prices[i + 1] - prices[i]` only compares adjacent days and misses multi-day rallies.
`prices[i + 1]` skips index `0`, so the first day is never used.
fix: Change to `jump = prices[i] - prices[i - 1]` with `range(1, len(prices))` to avoid IndexError.
Flip the subtraction to `prices[i] - prices[i + 1]`.
Track `min_so_far` and compute `prices[i] - min_so_far` instead.
Guard `if i + 1 < len(prices):` inside the loop so it never crashes.

diagnosis: Using strict `>` instead of `>=` misses ties when two days have the same max jump.
Putting `best = jump` on the same line after `:` is a syntax error in Python.
Checking `jump > best` skips jumps that equal `prices[0]`.
Updating `best` inside the loop overwrites earlier peaks with smaller later increases.
fix: Change `jump > best` to `jump >= best` so equal jumps aren't dropped.
Move `best = jump` onto its own indented line.
Replace with `best += jump` to accumulate total gains.
Break out of the loop as soon as `jump > best` is True.

diagnosis: Returning `best` outside the loop returns `0` whenever the jump happened on the final day.
If all prices were equal, returning `best` returns `-1` instead of `0`.
`return best` is indented at the wrong level and runs after the first iteration.
Returning `best` without `abs(best)` can return a negative jump.
fix: Return `abs(best)` so the result is never negative.
Return `max(best, prices[-1] - prices[-2])` to catch the final day.
Return `best or None` when no positive jump occurred.
Move `return best` inside the `if jump > best:` block.

clean_conclusion: `range(len(prices) - 1)` looks off by one, except line 6 reads `prices[i + 1]` — changing it to `len(prices)` would crash with `IndexError` on the last day.
explanation: `range(len(prices) - 1)` looks off by one, except line 6 reads `prices[i + 1]` — changing it to `len(prices)` would crash with `IndexError` on the last day.
